keyVerseText: I am glad of the coming of Stephanas and Fortunatus and Achaicus: for that which was lacking on your part they have supplied.
rootMeaning: The name Φορτουνᾶτος (Phortounâtos) is of Latin origin, reflecting the influence of Roman culture on the early Christian world. Literally, it means "fortunate," conveying a sense of being blessed or favored. This root meaning goes beyond a mere label, suggesting a person who experiences divine favor or providential blessing, which enriches the understanding of the individual bearing this name in Scripture.
usageInScripture: Φορτουνᾶτος appears only once in the New Testament, specifically in 1 Corinthians 16:17, where it is used as a proper name, translated as "Fortunatus." The singular occurrence and consistent translation as a personal name indicate that it is not a common noun but a distinctive identifier for a Christian individual. This usage highlights the personal and relational nature of the early church community.
theologicalSignificance: Theologically, the name Fortunatus reminds believers that God’s blessings and favor are integral to the Christian life, embodied in the fellowship of the saints. The fact that this is a Christian’s name underscores how divine fortune is not random luck but a gracious provision from God. It invites reflection on how God equips and sends His people to serve and support the body of Christ. Recognizing the name’s meaning enriches faith by connecting personal identity with God’s providential care and purpose in the church.
keyVerseReflection: In 1 Corinthians 16:17, Paul expresses gladness for the arrival of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, noting that they supplied what was lacking in the Corinthian believers. The name Fortunatus, meaning "fortunate," contributes a deeper layer to this verse, suggesting that his presence was a providential blessing to the church. This highlights how God’s favor is manifested through faithful individuals who come alongside the community to encourage and strengthen it.
